overview: The file documents U.S. State Department handling of Japanese press matters between 1931 and 1934. Most of the bundle concerns President Herbert Hoover’s congratulatory message to the Jiji-Shimpo on its fiftieth anniversary, including discussion of the precedent that presidential greetings to foreign newspapers might create, a draft tied to the newspaper’s goodwill mission of five Japanese women, White House approval, and instructions to the embassy in Tokyo to deliver the message. A final 1934 memorandum forwards an embassy despatch about the proposed, but not yet completed, amalgamation of Japan’s two principal news services.

people.name: French Strother
people.role: White House official conveying President Hoover’s instructions

subfiles.title: Castle to Strother concerning a presidential message to the Jiji-Shimpo
subfiles.about: Castle asks whether President Hoover wishes to congratulate the Jiji-Shimpo on its fiftieth anniversary despite the precedent this might establish for other foreign newspapers.
subfiles.summary: Associated Press representative Mr. Williamson reported that the King of England and other heads of state were sending anniversary messages to the Jiji-Shimpo and warned that Hoover’s absence would be conspicuous. Castle enclosed a suggested message but cautioned that Hoover had apparently never offered such congratulations to a foreign newspaper. He attempted to limit the precedent by connecting the greeting to the Jiji-Shimpo’s recent goodwill mission to the United States and offered to telegraph the embassy in Tokyo if the President approved.

subfiles.title: Draft congratulatory message from Hoover to the Jiji-Shimpo
subfiles.from: Herbert Hoover, drafted by the Department of State
subfiles.about: A proposed presidential message congratulates the Jiji-Shimpo on fifty years of journalism and praises its goodwill mission to the United States.
subfiles.summary: The draft congratulates the newspaper on completing fifty years of successful journalism. It describes the recent visit of five young Japanese women to the United States as evidence of the paper’s intention to foster cordial international relations.

subfiles.title: White House approval of the Jiji-Shimpo message
subfiles.about: Strother informs Castle that President Hoover approves sending the proposed congratulatory message to the Jiji-Shimpo.
subfiles.summary: Writing from the White House, Strother states that the President would be very glad for Castle to send the message enclosed with Castle’s letter earlier that day. The communication supplies the formal authorization needed for the State Department to transmit the greeting.

subfiles.title: Instruction to the Embassy in Tokyo to deliver Hoover’s message
subfiles.about: The Department instructs the embassy to deliver President Hoover’s congratulatory message immediately to the Jiji-Shimpo.
subfiles.summary: The telegram reproduces the approved presidential greeting and directs the embassy in Tokyo to deliver it immediately. Hoover congratulates the Jiji-Shimpo on fifty years of journalism and cites its goodwill mission of five Japanese women to the United States as a sign of support for cordial international relations.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on proposed amalgamation of Japanese news services
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: An internal memorandum forwards an embassy despatch concerning the proposed merger of Japan’s two principal news services.
subfiles.summary: The writer notes that a report from the military attaché in Tokyo on the proposed amalgamation had been forwarded several days earlier. A short embassy despatch on the same subject is now attached. The memorandum emphasizes that the amalgamation had not yet been consummated; the referenced despatch is not included in the surviving pages reproduced here.

interest: The file reveals the care with which the Hoover administration treated even a brief ceremonial message, particularly its concern that recognition of one foreign newspaper could establish an awkward diplomatic precedent. The papers also connect press diplomacy to the use of highly visible goodwill missions, including the visit of five Japanese women to the United States. The 1934 memorandum provides a separate glimpse of official American interest in the consolidation and organization of Japanese news distribution, although the reports and embassy despatch it references are absent from this bundle.
